study.title: Mark 7 - Purity of the heart, faith of the Gentiles, and healing that reveals the glory of Jesus
study.overview: Mark 7 brings together three main blocks: Jesus" controversy with Pharisees and scribes about religious tradition and ritual purity; the teaching that true contamination comes from the human interior; and two signs of mercy that show the reach and authority of Jesus. The chapter confronts the tendency to replace God's commandment with human practices, reveals that the central problem of the human being is not in food, but in the heart, and ends with healings that confirm the compassion of Christ and awaken public admiration.

outline.title: Human Tradition in conflict with God's commandment
outline.explanation: The Pharisees criticize the disciples for eating without ritual washing of their hands. Jesus responds by quoting Isaiah and denounces the hypocrisy of honoring God with his mouth while the heart is distant. It shows that religious traditions can nullify the divine commandment, using the case of the declared corbã offer to avoid the duty to care for parents.

outline.title: True impurity is born in the interior
outline.explanation: Jesus calls the crowd and teaches that nothing that enters the human being defils him spiritually; what comes out of him, yes, reveals and contaminates. To the disciples, he explains that food does not reach the heart, but moral evils arise from within, from the human heart, in the form of sinful thoughts and practices.

outline.title: Mercy for the Syrofenícia woman and healing of the deaf with difficulty to speak
outline.explanation: In Gentile territory, Jesus attends the humble persistence of a Greek woman of Syria and frees her daughter. Then, by healing a deaf man with difficulty of speech, Jesus acts in a personal and effective way, ordering discretion; even so, the people disclose the event and recognize that he does everything well.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the tension between Jesus and religious leaders of Jerusalem, who question practices of ritual purity and the tradition of the elders. The text explains these practices to non-Jewish readers, suggesting an audience that needed to understand Jewish customs. The narrative then shifts to regions associated with Gentiles, such as Tyre, Sidon and Decapolis, highlighting that the performance of Jesus goes beyond ethnic and religious boundaries.
study.theology: Mark 7 teaches that true holiness consists first of all in external rituals, but in obedience to God's commandment and inner transformation. Jesus does not despise the Law of God; on the contrary, he denounces the use of religious traditions when they empty the divine will, especially the duty to honor father and mother. The teaching on purity is radical: the moral impurity comes from the human heart, where perverse thoughts and actions spring. At the same time, the chapter shows the grace of Christ reaching a Gentile woman and her daughter, which points to the inclusion of non-Jews without the historical priority of Jesus' ministry to the Jewish people being denied. The final healings reveal that Jesus not only teaches correctly, but also fully restores, and the response of the multitude celebrates their perfect goodness and effectiveness.

scholarViews.insight: Mark explains the practices of ritual purification for non-Jewish readers and shows that the "traditions of the ancients" were customs accepted by the Pharisees as part of their religious heritage.
Religious tradition was used in order to dispense with the clear duty to support parents, so that the word of God was annulled by human custom.
The woman was Greek, that is, Gentile in Jewish eyes, and this observation highlights the scope of Jesus' meeting beyond Israel.

questions: In which areas of Christian life is there still the risk of giving more weight to the custom, tradition or human preference than to God's clear commandment?
What signs show, in everyday behavior itself, that the problem of sin comes from within and not just from external circumstances?
How does the persistent humility of the Christofenicia woman challenge our way of asking for help from Jesus?
study.practice: Examine your religious practices and ask if they really lead you to obedience to God's commandment or just preserve the appearance of pity. Confess that sin is not only external, but springs from the heart, and ask Christ to purify it. Imitate the humble faith of the Gentile woman, bringing their needs to the Lord with perseverance. Also learn from the crowd of Mark 7:37 to publicly recognize the goodness of Jesus: he does everything good, even when he acts unexpectedly.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided only offer excerpts, not full comments, so some nuances of each commentator may be absent. The identification of Tyre, Sidom and Decapolis in the context is accepted from the text itself and the notes, but broader historical details were not added because they were not provided. The expression Corbar is translated as an offering/consecrated to God, but the chapter does not develop all the legal implications of the term.
